bodyMarkdown:
## The idea in plain language

Some people in the puzzle always tell the truth, and others always lie. Someone says 'I am a liar' — which cannot be true, because a liar would not admit it, and a truth-teller would not say it.

That contradiction is the engine of the whole topic. You assume something, follow it through, and see whether the world it creates makes sense.

## What is actually going on

The reliable method is **assume and test**. Suppose person A is a truth-teller. Work out what every statement then implies. If you reach a contradiction, A must be a liar; if everything holds together, that scenario is possible.

Do this systematically rather than jumping between assumptions. Two people gives four cases; three gives eight — still perfectly countable.

Remember the asymmetry: a liar's statement is **false**, which tells you the opposite is true. A false statement is information, not an absence of it.

workedExamples.stemMarkdown: A says 'B is a liar'. B says 'A and I are both truth-tellers'. Who is what?
workedExamples.solutionMarkdown:
Assume A tells the truth. Then B is a liar, so B's claim must be false. B claimed both are truth-tellers — false, since B is a liar. Consistent so far, with no contradiction.

Now assume A lies. Then B is a truth-teller, so B's claim is true, meaning A is a truth-teller too. That contradicts our assumption that A lies.

So A is a truth-teller and B is a liar.
workedExamples.altSolutionMarkdown: Only one of the two assumptions survives — which is exactly how these puzzles are built.

formulaCards.title: Assume and test
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: Assume one person's type, follow every consequence, and reject the assumption if a contradiction appears.
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: If assuming A is truthful forces A to be lying, then A is a liar.

formulaCards.title: A lie is information
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: If a liar says X, then X is false, so the negation of X is true.
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: A liar saying 'C is guilty' establishes that C is not guilty.

commonTraps: Treating a liar's statement as merely unreliable. It is reliably false.
Stopping at the first consistent scenario without checking whether others also work.
Forgetting that 'not a truth-teller' means liar only when the puzzle offers exactly two types.
